title: A letter for after
hook: a letter to be read after you're gone

segments.voice: Yesterday, a skull on a painter's desk and Hamlet in the graveyard. Your line was an object to remember. Did your object catch your eye today? Today, something you leave behind on purpose: words. Day eight hundred ten.

An envelope in a drawer, with one line on the front: to be opened after I'm gone. Inside there's no list of bank accounts and nothing about who gets the good chairs. Just a page about what the writer learned, what they hope for, what they'd like forgiven. In Jewish tradition this kind of letter has a name, an ethical will, and some families still write and keep them. The idea is far older than envelopes. Today: the letter for after, and a few people in old books who wrote one out loud.
screen: `TO BE OPENED AFTER I'M GONE.` → `NO MONEY, NO CHAIRS.` → `AN ETHICAL WILL.`

segments.voice: First, Jacob gathers his sons. In Genesis, the old man calls his family to his bed: "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days." What follows is a long speech to each son by name. Some of it is blessing and some of it is blunt. It isn't a will about property. It's a father saying who he thinks each of them is. Second, a farewell. In the second letter to Timothy, the writer sounds like someone near the end: "the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Some readers hear the whole letter as a farewell, written for after. Third, a will made of words. The Hebrew word for a will is tsavaah, and the ethical will borrows it for something different: not who gets what, but what mattered. Some are a few sentences long. Some are pages of advice, apology and thanks. Rabbis wrote them, and so did ordinary parents. Fourth, first lines only. Nobody needs to write the whole letter today. A first line is enough to find out what you'd want to say. And once a line is written for after, it has a way of asking whether it could be said now.
screen: `JACOB GATHERS HIS SONS.` · `A FAREWELL TO TIMOTHY.` · `A WILL MADE OF WORDS.` · `FIRST LINES ONLY.` · then, large: `A LETTER FOR AFTER.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and paper, or a note on your phone. Think of one person who might one day read a letter from you. Don't plan the whole thing. Let the first lines come: maybe what you hope for them, or one thing you learned, or one thing you're grateful for. Write two or three sentences, no more. If nothing comes, write their name and sit with it. Then put it somewhere safe, or simply let it go. The bell holds the time.
A letter for after. Words written to be read once you're gone, like Jacob's blessings or a Jewish ethical will: not property, but what mattered. Today's word.
Your line: after me. Today, read your first lines once more, and ask whether any of them could be said to that person sooner. Day eight hundred ten.

howItsDone: In Jewish tradition, an ethical will, a tsavaah, is a letter of values, blessings and requests left for family; some people of other paths also write letters to be read after their death, sometimes kept with a legal will.
